# [Capital Chronicle](https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/)

# September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions

### In its October 14 release on September 2026 CPI, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported monthly and annual readings with different horizons and adjustment bases.

[Capital Chronicle's avatar](https://substack.com/@capitalchronicle)[Capital Chronicle](https://substack.com/@capitalchronicle)6 hours ago

September 2026's headline CPI rose 0.6% over one month and 3.7% over twelve months, according to the [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics release of October 14, 2026](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_10142026.htm). The monthly figure is seasonally adjusted; the annual figure is not. They describe different horizons. This retrospective puts that release alongside the earlier readings and its component breakdown.

[Bags of dry beans displayed on shelves at a supermarket in Dearborn, Michigan.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G8nN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb60973f2-b9d3-45de-b0ba-4c676839f7c4_5364x3334.jpeg)
*.[USDAgov / U.S. Department of Agriculture, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (17 USC 105).](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WIC_Environments_in_Michigan_(20230621-USDA-FNS-UNK-0020).jpg)*

## What the annual history shows

The dated BLS releases show different paths over the 24-month window. Headline annual inflation was 2.6% in October 2024 and 3.7% in September 2026. Core was 3.3% and 2.6%, respectively. Headline reached 4.2% in May 2026 before the September reading; the path was uneven.

[Two lines show first-reported annual CPI-U inflation from October 2024 to September 2026, with a gap at October 2025. Headline starts at 2.6%, reaches 4.2% in May 2026 and ends at 3.7%. Core starts at 3.3% and ends at 2.6%.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!t6Lv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcafc7b1b-e673-40ed-a16f-5024435e8fa8_1440x1040.png)
*U.S. CPI-U, twelve-month change, not seasonally adjusted, October 2024-September 2026. Each point uses its first published reading. October 2025 has no published reading. Source: BLS dated CPI releases.*

Core excludes food and energy. Its lower annual reading describes that narrower basket. It does not establish how long the pressure in the full basket would last.

## The monthly pace

In the October 14 release, September's monthly headline increase was 0.6%, following 0.4% in August. Core rose 0.3% in both months. At the published precision, the latest monthly pace increased in headline CPI while core's pace held steady.

[Two lines show first-reported monthly, seasonally adjusted CPI-U changes from October 2024 to September 2026. Both lines break at October and November 2025. September 2026 headline inflation is 0.6%, following 0.4% in August; core is 0.3% in both months.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Baoy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5db3290-9d38-4eb3-9b3c-19508af49720_1440x1040.png)
*U.S. CPI-U, one-month change, seasonally adjusted, October 2024-September 2026. These are first-release vintages. October and November 2025 have no one-month readings; November's release covered two months. Source: BLS dated CPI releases.*

The history charts preserve each month's first reading in its dated BLS release. The monthly chart therefore follows successive release vintages, rather than today's revised seasonally adjusted history. Its breaks preserve the months without published one-month readings.

## What contributed to September's increase

BLS Table 6 supplies the component effects that the headline-core gap alone cannot identify. Energy contributed 0.377 percentage points to the all-items monthly change, core contributed 0.265 points and food contributed 0.006 points. Energy was the largest of these broad contributions, while core also added to the increase.

[Horizontal bars show September 2026 seasonally adjusted effects on all-items monthly CPI-U inflation: energy 0.377 percentage points, core excluding food and energy 0.265 points, and food 0.006 points. Energy has the largest broad contribution.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VdUh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb13fb2a5-f023-4c78-8cff-23d99cb05ee5_1440x1040.png)
*Reported effects on all-items CPI-U, August-September 2026, seasonally adjusted, in percentage points. The three broad categories do not overlap. Effects retain BLS's three-decimal precision; the headline monthly rate is published as 0.6%. Source: BLS, October 14, 2026 release, Table 6.*

# [Capital Chronicle](https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/)

# The Fed held on October 28. Both dissenters wanted a hike.

### A 10-2 vote kept the federal funds target at 3.75 to 4 percent. The dissenters wanted an increase; the companion note explains the operating settings.

[Capital Chronicle's avatar](https://substack.com/@capitalchronicle)[Capital Chronicle](https://substack.com/@capitalchronicle)16 hours ago[Archive portrait of Kevin Warsh in a navy suit at his May 22, 2026 swearing-in ceremony.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O9EE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb4c81a31-fde0-48c2-a1b7-c963f175745d_635x900.jpeg)
*Photo: [The White House](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Federal_Reserve_Chair_Kevin_Warsh_delivers_remarks_at_his_swearing-in_ceremony_in_the_East_Room_of_the_White_House,_Friday,_May_22,_2026._(Cropped).jpg) · [Reuse terms](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-USGov). Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at his May 22, 2026 swearing-in ceremony. Archive context; this is not a photograph of the October 28 decision. Official White House photograph by Daniel Torok, May 22, 2026. Public domain (US federal government). Commons crop; no further edits.*

*Retrospective analysis, written on 1 November 2026 (GMT+7).*

An unchanged rate can still contain a pointed disagreement. On October 28, 2026, the Federal Reserve’s policy committee voted 10-2 to keep the federal funds target range at 3.75 to 4 percent, according to its [October 28 statement](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm). Both dissenters wanted a quarter-percentage-point increase.

Capital Chronicle’s reading is that the decision and its implementation answer different questions. The vote establishes the target range and the direction of disagreement. The companion note sets out the rates and instructions used to implement that stance. A reader needs both documents to distinguish the policy choice from its operating settings.

## A hold with dissent in one direction

[October 28, 2026 FOMC vote: 10 members approved holding the target range; 2 members, Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, preferred a quarter-percentage-point increase. Horizontal member-count axis starts at zero.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GxK5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7aec59ba-4da6-4e6c-a6b9-767eb96e1798_1500x1300.png)
*The October 28 vote: 10 members approved a hold; Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. Sources: [Federal Reserve Board](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm).*

Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted against the action because they preferred to raise the target range by a quarter percentage point at that meeting. That makes the direction of dissent clear: they favored an increase, while the approved action maintained the range.

The statement described economic activity as expanding strongly, domestic spending as resilient and inflation as elevated. It also said accumulating more information would help the Committee determine the stance appropriate for a timely return to its 2 percent inflation goal. That is the Committee’s published assessment; it should not be turned into a separate explanation attributed to either dissenter.

The strongest countercase to a looming-hike interpretation is the decision itself: ten members approved keeping the range unchanged. The two dissenters’ preference is evidence of disagreement at this meeting, not a forecast of the next vote. Reading the split as a timetable for higher rates would give it a meaning the vote alone cannot establish.

## One target range, several operating rates

[Announced October 28, 2026: federal funds target interval 3.75 to 4.00 percent; reserve interest 3.90; standing overnight reverse repo 3.75; standing overnight repo 4.00; existing primary credit 4.00. These are announced settings, not observed market rates. Reserve interest and the operating directive effective October 29.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Ts0!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3eda43e3-d024-4867-8a3e-3d64e98433c5_1500x1300.png)
*The target range and individual operating settings announced October 28. Reserve interest and the operating directive were effective October 29; primary credit was at its existing level. Sources: [Federal Reserve Board](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm); [Federal Reserve Board](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a1.htm).*
